HSTU already supports the proposed direction: its relative attention bias combines positional distance with temporal information, including bucketized timestamp differences. Bias enters the SiLU attention calculation; attention-pooled values then pass through normalization and multiplicative gating. Thus, learned time-gap effects fit within the HSTU backbone without requiring another predictor. The original results establish architectural precedent, but do not establish gains for sparse histories under this benchmark. [HSTU, ICML 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17152v3)

Related work supports distinguishing interaction order from elapsed time. TemProxRec (2024) combines absolute and relative temporal/positional embeddings with temporal-proximity contrastive learning. HeteroTempRec (2026) investigates adaptive weighting of short- and long-term preferences, though its different architecture provides only indirect support for an HSTU modification. Neither establishes that stronger recency weighting universally improves sparse-history prediction. [TemProxRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784), [HeteroTempRec](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020025525008369)

Experiment implication—an inference from these sources: jointly learn bucketed pairwise time-gap biases and a small context-conditioned recency gate inside each category’s single HSTU model. Use observed-prefix timestamps only; during training, compute recency relative to each causal query, never a later event or unknown next-item timestamp. Preserve older-interest access rather than imposing universal decay. Compare temporal bias alone against bias plus gating using the fixed macro validation HR@10. Omitted paired-context effects remain unknown; they provide no evidence that the corrected baseline lacks recency sensitivity.
